newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish soldiers jailed for links to Kurd rebels.
newsitem.headline: Turkish soldiers jailed for links to Kurd rebels.

text.p: A Turkish court in Ankara on Monday jailed two army staff sergeants for seven-and-a-half years each for giving military information and equipment to Kurdish guerrillas, Anatolian news agency said.

The agency also said the Ankara security court had opened a case against four Kurdish former deputies from a now closed pro-Kurdish party on similar charges stemming from their time as MPs in the early 1990s.
The soldiers, Mehmet Peker and Ibrahim Dag, were found guilty of aiding the Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) rebel group. They denied the charge.

"They betrayed the army they belonged to by giving information on army operations and sending army equipment to the armed bandits trying to divide the country," the agency quoted the charge sheet as saying.
Turkey's large army is made up mostly of conscripts but the pair were full-time professional soldiers based at two towns in western Turkey, far from the PKK's normal area of operation.

Security forces killed 17 PKK guerrillas in the latest clashes in the southeastern provinces of Hakkari, Mardin, Van, Bingol and Sirnak, the emergency rule governor's office in the city of Diyarbakir said in a statement.
The statement did not say when the clashes took place.
More than 21,000 people have been killed in the conflict in southeast Turkey between security forces and the rebels, fighting for Kurdish self-rule since 1984.
Anatolian said three former MPs, Mehmet Emin Sever, Mahmut Uyanik and Muzaffer Demir, faced between 4.5 and 7.5 years in jail for allegedly aiding the PKK.
A fourth former deputy, Abdulkerim Zilan, was charged with spreading separatist propaganda for which he could face one to three years in jail. The former deputies have not been detained.

The four defendants caused an uproar in Turkey's parliament in 1991 when they wore to the swearing-in ceremony handkerchiefs in yellow, red and green -- Kurdish colours identified by many in Turkey with the PKK.

Accusations against them also include going on a hunger strike to protest against anti-rebel military operations in the southeast and holding a news conference in 1991 to protest at the deputies' oath, which they said was a denial of the existence of the Kurdish people.
It was unclear why the court took so long to charge them.
Their Kurdish-based HEP (People's Labour Party) was outlawed for separatism by the constitutional court in July 1993.
